When the Calder Street branch library in Redhaven reopened after its refit, the council expected a crowd. None came: the door counter recorded as many visitors as before. What changed was how long they stayed: visits of over an hour roughly doubled. Two sociologists, Ostrander and Njoku, spent two years finding out why.

Four changes could each explain the pattern; three did not survive. The longer hours cannot explain it: the added time came in the evening, but the new visits end before six. The doorway now faces the market square, but the newcomers come from the streets behind and never make that walk. What remains is the rule at the door: the card check was dropped, and nearly every new long visitor carries no card.

Proving the change real meant settling an old question: the logbook's fourth column is headed Reserve, a word this town uses in four ways. In that heading it does not mean the duplicate volumes held back from the shelves; it does not mean the woodland reserve at the parish edge; it does not mean a room claimed in advance. It means the repair fund kept against the roof, a sum set aside year by year, so the column recorded money rather than readers.

Who stayed? Not people working at home, who would come any weekday alike, when the rise stops in the school holidays. Not shoppers from the market, who would come on market days alone, when the rise is even. Not the depot's early-shift workers, who are at their machines until six. The Fenwick branch, in the next town, entered the study because the local logbook counted money rather than readers: the earlier figures had to come from its unbroken records. It was not brought in to rule out a rival explanation, nor to show the pattern in a second town, nor to fix the limits of the claim.
